# 2026-11-22: Erasing a mechanical bit, and the cost of a cycle {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
**Status:** exploratory · **Thread:** T7 · **Checked by:** `tests/test_erasure.py`
:::

**Question.** A body that records events over and over must clear each record before it can
take the next one. The notes on [writing](2026-11-22-writing-a-bit.qmd) and on
[a bit inside a body](2026-11-22-bit-in-a-body.qmd) covered writing and reading. What does
erasing cost, and what does a full write-read-erase cycle cost?

**Short answer.**

- *Erasing has a floor.* Resetting a bit whose value is unknown to a fixed well costs, on
    average, at least $\sigma_T^2\ln2\approx0.69\,\sigma_T^2$ of work (Landauer's bound),
    because the body ends up knowing less about where the element might be. A reset that
    is allowed an error $p$ needs at least $\sigma_T^2(\ln2-H(p))$.
- *The simulated erasure reaches it slowly.* Lowering the barrier, tilting toward the
    target, raising the barrier and removing the tilt costs $1.37\,\sigma_T^2$ when each
    stage lasts 5 time units and $0.695\,\sigma_T^2$ when each lasts 200. The excess falls
    like $1/\tau$, as measured in colloidal experiments.
- *Slow erasure leaks.* The slowest erasure leaves 1.2% of bits in the wrong well, against
    0.15% for the fastest, because the element has time to cross back. Speed, cost and
    accuracy trade against each other.
- *In a cycle, the write dominates.* A write driven by the environment's push costs about
    $3.6\Delta E\approx29\,\sigma_T^2$ at a barrier of $8\,\sigma_T^2$, forty times the
    erasure floor. Reading by another part of the body costs no work. Landauer's bound
    applies only to the erasure.

## Setting

The element of the bit notes in the book's units (lengths $a$, energies $\sigma_T^2$, times
$\sqrt{ma^2/\sigma_T^2}$), damping rate $\gamma=2$, written as
$$
U(x,t)=\beta x^4-a_2(t)\,x^2-f(t)\,x ,
$$
which is the double well $\beta\big((x^2-1)^2-1\big)$ with barrier $\beta=8$ when
$a_2=2\beta$ and $f=0$. The bit starts in a random well, each with probability one half, at
equilibrium inside its well. The erasure resets it to the left well in four stages of equal
length $\tau$ [@berut2012experimental]:

1. lower the barrier, $a_2$ from $2\beta$ to 0;
2. tilt to the left, $f$ from 0 to $-5$, so that the right side ends 10 thermal energies
    higher;
3. raise the barrier, $a_2$ from 0 back to $2\beta$;
4. remove the tilt, $f$ from $-5$ to 0.

The work is the energy put in by changing the potential, summed along each trajectory as
$U(x,t+dt)-U(x,t)$ at the current position. Each value of $\tau$ uses 2,000 elements.

## Results

::: {#prp-landauer name="Landauer's bound, with errors"}
Reset an element whose well is equally likely to be left or right, so that afterwards it is
in the right well with probability $p\le\frac12$, and both wells have the same shape at the
start and the end. The mean work satisfies
$$
\langle W\rangle\ \ge\ \sigma_T^2\big(\ln2-H(p)\big),\qquad H(p)=-p\ln p-(1-p)\ln(1-p),
$$
which is $\sigma_T^2\ln2$ for a perfect reset.
:::

::: {.proof name="Proof sketch"}
*Step 1: the second law far from equilibrium.* For the Langevin body with a potential
changed in time, the mean work exceeds the change in nonequilibrium free energy,
$\langle W\rangle\ge\Delta\mathcal F$, where $\mathcal F=\langle U\rangle-\sigma_T^2S$ and $S$ is
the entropy of the distribution of the state [@esposito2011second]. The difference is
$\sigma_T^2$ times the entropy produced, which is never negative.

*Step 2: the start and the end.* The potential is the same at both ends. Inside each well
the element is at local equilibrium, and the two wells are mirror images, so the mean
energy is the same before and after. Only the occupation of the wells changes: from
$(\frac12,\frac12)$, with entropy $\ln2$, to $(1-p,p)$, with entropy $H(p)$. So
$\Delta\mathcal F=\sigma_T^2(\ln2-H(p))$.

*What is not proved here.* Step 1 is quoted; the end state is taken to be at local
equilibrium inside each well, which holds when the barrier is high.
:::

The bound counts the work against the information the body loses about where the element
could be. Writing into a known starting state, as in the writing note, loses no such
information, and Landauer's bound does not apply to it. Reading the bit by another part of
the body, as in the bit-in-a-body note, needs no work at all: the part simply moves with the
body. That is the classical position of Bennett [@bennett1982thermodynamics]: measuring can be
free, and the cost appears when a record is erased.

## Numbers

```{python}
#| label: fig-erasure
#| fig-cap: |
#|   (a) Mean work of the four-stage erasure against the length of each stage, with two
#|   standard errors, the fit $W_\infty+B/\tau$ to the three slowest runs, and Landauer's bound.
#|   (b) Share of elements left in the wrong well.
from mibook import figures
figures.fig_erasure();
```

| stage length $\tau$ | 5 | 10 | 20 | 50 | 100 | 200 |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| mean work / $\sigma_T^2$ | 1.372 | 1.015 | 0.862 | 0.758 | 0.720 | 0.695 |
| standard error | 0.027 | 0.020 | 0.014 | 0.010 | 0.008 | 0.006 |
| in the wrong well | 0.15% | 0.25% | 0.10% | 0.45% | 0.60% | 1.20% |
| bound at that error | 0.682 | 0.676 | 0.685 | 0.664 | 0.657 | 0.628 |

: The four-stage erasure at a barrier of $8\,\sigma_T^2$ (`check_erasure`). The bound is $\ln2-H(p)$ at the measured error $p$. {#tbl-erasure}

- Every run costs more than its bound, by 0.07 $\sigma_T^2$ at $\tau=200$ and by 0.69 at
    $\tau=5$.
- A fit $W=W_\infty+B/\tau$ to the three slowest runs gives $W_\infty=0.675$ and $B=4.2$. The
    limit lies a little under $\ln2=0.693$ because the slow runs leave more errors, which
    lowers their bound.
- The errors grow with $\tau$ because the bit has more time to leak back over the barrier
    while the tilt is removed. At this barrier the flip rate of the untilted well is about
    $3.6\times10^{-4}$ per time unit (from the bit note), so over the last stage of the
    slowest run, 200 time units during which the tilt fades, errors of a few tenths of a
    percent up to a few percent are expected; the measured 1.2% lies in that range.

**The cost of a cycle at a barrier of $8\,\sigma_T^2$.**

| step | work | how it is done here |
|:--|--:|:--|
| write | $\approx29\,\sigma_T^2$ ($3.6\Delta E$) | a steady push at $1.1F_c$, 98.5% reliable |
| read | 0 | another part moves with the body |
| erase | $0.70$ to $1.37\,\sigma_T^2$ | the four-stage protocol, $\tau=200$ to 5 |

: Work per cycle; Landauer's bound applies only to the erasure, $0.69\,\sigma_T^2$. {#tbl-cycle}

## What this changes

A mechanical memory has a thermodynamic price, and this note puts numbers on it. Erasure is
the only step with a hard floor, $\sigma_T^2\ln2$, and a slow protocol reaches it, at the cost
of time and of some accuracy, since a slow erasure gives the bit time to leak. The step that
dominates in practice is the write, because the environment pushes fast and the energy that
carries the element over the barrier is then dissipated. On the book's effective temperature
scale a write costs tens of thermal energies and an erasure about one. This is the first
link in the book between mechanical intelligence and the thermodynamics of computation.

## Limits of this note

- One protocol, one barrier, one tilt and one damping rate. Optimal protocols for a given
    time, which lower the $1/\tau$ term, are not explored.
- The bound's proof quotes the second law for nonequilibrium free energy.
- The write's cost is that of the push used in the writing note, not a minimum over ways
    of writing.
- The element is on its own; erasing a bit inside a body, where the body pushes back,
    would change the barrier and the protocol.
